subject: zoology

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.64, SAQ 179). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. ADDED BEYOND THE BOOK: the transport of absorbed fats and the defence role of the lymphocytes are standard NCERT content and are not printed in this book's answer.

steps.label: What lymph is
steps.why: Lymph and interstitial fluid are the same fluid in two places, so the definition has to say WHERE it is rather than what it is made of.
common_mistakes: Calling lymph blood without red cells. It is tissue fluid that has entered the lymph vessels.
Writing that it flows in the blood vessels. It has its own vessels.
steps.memory_tip: Same fluid, two names: interstitial fluid between the cells, lymph once it is in a lymph vessel.
steps.margin_note: Colour, where it flows, what it is. Two or three lines.
lines: Lymph is a colourless fluid that flows through
the vessels of the lymphatic system.
It is the interstitial fluid, the fluid lying in
the spaces between the cells, once it has
entered a lymph vessel.

steps.label: How lymph is formed
steps.why: Lymph exists because more fluid leaves the capillaries than returns to them, and the lymph vessels collect the small amount that is left behind.
common_mistakes: Writing that lymph is made by the lymph glands. It is filtered out of the blood capillaries.
Leaving out hydrostatic pressure, which is what drives the fluid out.
steps.memory_tip: Pressure pushes fluid out of the capillary; most of it goes back, and the small remainder becomes lymph.
steps.margin_note: Pressure, fluid out, most back, a little into lymph vessels. Four short lines.
lines: Blood entering a capillary is under pressure,
called hydrostatic pressure.
This pressure drives water, nutrients, oxygen
and other small materials out of the capillary
into the spaces between the cells.
Most of this fluid returns to the blood at the
far end of the capillary.
A small part of it enters the lymph capillaries
and becomes lymph.

steps.label: What lymph contains
steps.why: Everything present in lymph is what could pass through the capillary wall and everything missing is what was too large to pass, so one rule explains the whole list.
common_mistakes: Writing that lymph has no cells. It carries lymphocytes.
Saying it is richer in oxygen than blood. It carries less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.
steps.memory_tip: Too big to cross the capillary wall stays behind: red cells, platelets and large proteins.
steps.margin_note: What is in it, what is missing, and how it compares with blood.
lines: Lymph is made of plasma and lymphocytes.
It has no red blood cells and no platelets.
It carries less protein than plasma, because the
large plasma proteins cannot cross the capillary
wall.
It carries less oxygen and fewer nutrients than
blood, and more carbon dioxide and other waste
products.

steps.label: Where lymph goes back
steps.why: The lymphatic system is a one-way road with a single exit, and naming that exit turns a list of facts into a circuit the examiner can follow.
common_mistakes: Writing that lymph circulates like blood. It flows one way only, from the tissues back to the veins.
Leaving out the words accessory route, which is what this book's answer closes with.
steps.memory_tip: One-way street: tissues, then lymph vessels, then the subclavian veins, then the blood.
steps.margin_note: Name the subclavian veins and the words accessory route. Close with the two extra jobs.

lines.text: Lymph rejoins the blood at the subclavian veins

lines: The lymph vessels join one another and finally
open into the subclavian veins near the heart.
So the fluid that left the capillaries is
returned to the blood.
The lymphatic system is therefore called an
accessory route back to the blood.
Lymph also carries fats absorbed from the
intestine, and its lymphocytes defend the body.

insider_note: 'Short notes' still means four blocks for four marks — what it is, how it forms, what it holds, where it goes — and the return at the subclavian veins is the line most papers never reach.
